draft.title: Census, sample, experiment, observation
card: collects data from every member of a population. It gives the full picture, but it can take a lot of time and money.
collects data from only part of a population. It is quicker and cheaper, but the results may not match the whole population exactly.
changes one thing on purpose and records what happens, such as trying two fertilisers on plants. It can be hard to control everything else.
watches and records what happens without changing anything, such as counting cars at an intersection. It may only show what happened on that day.
draft.remember: Census asks everyone, a sample asks some, an experiment changes something, and an observation only watches.

a.q: A shire council wants to know how many of its 400 staff cycle to work. It asks every one of the 400 staff. What method is this?
a.why: Every member of the population of 400 staff is asked, so it is a census. It is not a sample, because a sample uses only part of the population.
a.clue: Count how many of the staff are asked.

b.q: Tariq stands at a school gate in Ballarat for one morning and tallies how many students arrive by bus. He does not speak to anyone. What method is this?
b.why: Tariq only watches and records, and he changes nothing, so it is an observation. It would be an experiment only if he changed something on purpose, such as offering a reward to see if more students took the bus.
b.clue: Did Tariq change anything or ask anyone?
